planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; unlike most wood ferns, tolerates and even prefers consistently damp to boggy soil, making it a good choice for the edges of shaded rain gardens or stream banks.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Tokyo wood fern is immediately distinctive among Dryopteris for its stiffly upright, narrow, sword-like fronds that form a strict vase-shaped clump rather than the softer arching habit typical of most wood ferns, giving it a strong vertical accent in shaded plantings. It is deciduous, dying back after hard frost, and emerges again reliably each spring. It tolerates wetter soil than nearly any other Dryopteris, so it pairs well with moisture-loving companions like Osmunda and Athyrium at pond edges or in low, damp woodland areas.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial sun to light shade in spring; give it good drainage and it will reward you with glossy, leathery fronds that persist through winter in milder zones.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial sun to light shade. Native to Japan, Korea, and China, Champion's wood fern is prized for its dark, glossy green, bipinnate fronds that hold their color and texture better than many wood ferns, remaining evergreen to semi-evergreen through mild winters. Its upright, arching habit and unusually shiny leaf surface make it stand out as a specimen plant against duller-textured shade perennials. It combines well with hostas and hellebores in a woodland border where its glossy foliage catches available light.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist but well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; once established it tolerates dry shade better than many colorful-flushing ferns.

directions: Plant in moist but well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Sunset fern earns its common name from new fronds that emerge a striking salmon-pink to orange-red before shifting through yellow and finally settling into dark green as they mature, giving the clump a slow-motion color show through the growing season. The clump-forming, evergreen to semi-evergreen habit stays tidy without spreading aggressively. It tolerates dry shade once established, making it a useful color accent under trees where moisture-loving ferns often struggle.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade in spring; forms a tidy non-spreading clump that requires no division for many years.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade. Korean lady fern is a woodland native of Japan, Korea, and China closely related to the common lady fern, but distinguished by its deep reddish-burgundy stipes (leaf stalks) that contrast handsomely with the fresh green, finely divided fronds. It forms a neat, non-spreading clump rather than colonizing outward, so it stays well behaved in mixed shade borders. Deciduous and deer-resistant, it combines well with hostas, hellebores, and other Athyrium species for a layered woodland planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade after the last frost; provide winter mulch at the cold end of its range since it is only semi-evergreen and less cold-hardy than Cyrtomium fortunei.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Bigleaf holly fern is native to a wide swath of Asia from the Himalayas to southeastern China at fairly high elevation, which gives it more cold tolerance than the tropical look of its bold, undivided, yellow-green pinnae would suggest. Each arching frond carries just a few large, glossy leaflets rather than the many small leaflets typical of most ferns, giving the plant a coarse, tropical texture that contrasts well with fine-textured neighbors. It is semi-evergreen, so older fronds often look tattered by late winter and are best cut back to let fresh new growth take over in spring.

planting.note: Tuck small divisions or container plants into crevices of a stone wall, rock garden, or tufa in gritty, alkaline, sharply drained soil in partial shade; established plants need very little supplemental water.

directions: Plant in gritty, alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil tucked into crevices of a stone wall, dry rock garden, or tufa in partial shade. Rustyback fern is a diminutive European rock fern named for the dense coppery-brown scales that coat the undersides of its narrow, lobed fronds. It is unusually drought tolerant for a fern: in dry spells the fronds curl inward and appear shriveled and dead, then uncurl and green up again within days of rain, a resurrection trick most ferns cannot perform. Its small scale and love of lime-rich crevices make it a specialty plant for dry stone walls and rock gardens rather than a general woodland-border fern.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade sheltered from wind and never allowed to drop below about 40F; very slow growing, so allow years for a trunk to develop.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, sheltered from drying wind. Hapu'u pulu is the most common native tree fern of the Hawaiian rainforest understory, forming a shaggy fibrous trunk topped by a broad crown of arching fronds; the soft, golden-brown wool at the base of new fronds was historically harvested for pillow and mattress stuffing. It is extremely slow growing and needs constant moisture and warmth year-round, making it best suited to frost-free coastal or tropical gardens, greenhouses, or large protected courtyards elsewhere. Give it plenty of overhead room, since a mature specimen eventually forms a substantial trunk and broad crown.
sources: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife (DLNR)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, protected from wind and frost; the largest of the Hawaiian tree ferns and needs generous long-term space.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, sheltered from wind. Hapu'u 'i'i is endemic to the island of Hawai'i and is the largest of the native Hawaiian tree ferns, eventually forming a thick, tall trunk topped by huge arching fronds. It is distinguished from the similar Cibotium glaucum by coarse, dark, bristle-like hairs at the base of new fronds rather than soft golden wool. In its native rainforest it serves as a keystone habitat plant, its trunk and crown hosting numerous epiphytic ferns and other plants; in cultivation it demands the same constant warmth and moisture, making it suitable only for frost-free tropical gardens or large conservatories.
sources: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife (DLNR)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade, sheltered from wind that can shred the huge fronds; allow substantial space, as the rhizome and frond spread expand considerably over years.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade, sheltered from wind. The giant king fern is an ancient, primitive species in the Marattiaceae, a lineage that predates most modern fern families, and it produces what are believed to be the longest fronds of any fern in the world, arching outward from a massive, trunk-like rhizome. It needs constant warmth and moisture and cannot tolerate frost, so it is grown outdoors only in true tropical climates or as a dramatic specimen in large conservatories and shaded courtyards elsewhere. Give it generous overhead and lateral space, since the rhizome and frond crown both expand substantially as the plant matures over many years.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade, protected from frost and drying wind; give the massive fleshy rhizome room to expand over years.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade, protected from frost and drying wind. King fern (also classified as Ptisana salicina) is a large, ancient fern native to New Zealand, Norfolk Island, and the South Pacific, forming a massive fleshy rhizome topped by huge, broad, once- to twice-divided fronds up to several meters long. It was historically an important food plant for the Maori, who harvested and cooked the starchy rhizome. It needs steady warmth, shelter from wind, and constant moisture, making it best suited to frost-free subtropical to tropical gardens or large sheltered conservatories.
